summary: Defines how audio from the ITU-T G.722.1 wide-band codec is carried in RTP packets. It also gives the SDP parameters needed to announce and negotiate use of the codec in a session.

eli5.summary: A wide-band codec captures sound in rich detail. This document says how to pack that sound into small network parcels and how to write the note telling the receiver what is inside.

questions: how is g.722.1 carried in rtp
what sdp parameters does g7221 use
what bit rates does g.722.1 support
subtitle: How to pack G.722.1 wide-band audio frames into RTP packets and describe them in SDP.

tldr.problem: G.722.1 is a wide-band audio codec, but its bit stream does not say its own bit rate, and sending it over RTP needs agreed rules for packing frames and announcing the settings.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP payload carries one or more whole G.722.1 frames, octet-aligned and unchanged from the encoder output. The bit rate and clock rate are fixed per payload type and signaled out of band, using the audio/G7221 media type and SDP.
tldr.outcome: This document obsoletes RFC 3047 and adds support for the 32 kHz (superwideband) mode defined in annex C of the new revision of G.722.1.

today: RFC 5577 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3047. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: The G.722.1 Codec
sections.content:
ITU-T G.722.1 is a low-complexity coder that compresses 50 Hz to 14 kHz audio into one of three bit rates: 24 kbit/s, 32 kbit/s or 48 kbit/s. It may be used for speech, music and other audio, with suggested uses such as videoconferencing and telephony, streaming audio, and archival and messaging.

It works on 20-ms frames with a sampling clock of 16 kHz or 32 kHz. The bit rate can change at any frame boundary, but nothing in the bit stream announces the change. For a given bit rate, the number of bits in a frame is constant, and most parameters inside it use variable-length (Huffman) codes sent from the most significant bit to the least significant bit.

The standardized rates are 24 and 32 kbit/s at 16 kHz, and 24, 32 or 48 kbit/s at 32 kHz. The algorithm can also run at other user-specified rates, scaling linearly, which gives frames of 1/50 of the bit rate in bits.
sections.eli5: The codec listens to sound in tiny 20-millisecond slices and squeezes each slice into a small, fixed-size bundle of bits.

sections.title: RTP Header Fields
sections.content:
The RTP header is defined in RFC 3550, and this document only says how some fields are used.

  • Payload type: assigning one is outside the scope of this document. It comes from the RTP profile in use or is signaled dynamically out of band, for example with SDP.
  • Marker (M) bit: set to zero.
  • Extension (X) bit: defined by the RTP profile used.
  • Timestamp: a 32-bit word for the sampling instant of the first frame in the packet. The sampling frequency can be 16 kHz or 32 kHz, and a timestamp clock of 32 kHz SHOULD be used unless only a 16 kHz stream will be sent.
sections.eli5: Most of the packet label is filled in the usual RTP way. The special rules are small: the marker is always zero, and the clock should tick at the faster speed unless the sound is the slower kind.

sections.title: The Payload Format
sections.content:
The payload is just one or more G.722.1 frames after the RTP header. No payload-specific header fields are needed.

Because the bit rate is not signaled in the stream, a separate out-of-band method is REQUIRED to indicate it. The bit rate MUST stay constant for a given payload type value. An application MAY change bit rates and clock rates between packets by defining several payload types and switching among them.

Huffman coding means the fields cannot be identified without decoding the whole frame. So the packetizer simply keeps the sequence of bits exactly as the encoder produced it and presents the same sequence to the decoder. At the standard rates a frame is 480 bits (60 octets) at 24 kbit/s, 640 bits (80 octets) at 32 kbit/s and 960 bits (120 octets) at 48 kbit/s, so no padding bits are needed.

For non-standard rates, values in the range 16000 to 48000 are RECOMMENDED, and the rate MUST be a multiple of 400 to stay octet aligned. For example, 16.4 kbit/s gives a frame of 328 bits or 41 octets.
sections.eli5: The bits go into the parcel in exactly the order the codec made them, like stacking blocks without shuffling. The sizes are chosen so the blocks always fit whole bytes.

sections.title: Multiple Frames per Packet
sections.content:
A sender may put more than one consecutive frame in a single RTP packet, within these limits:

  • It SHOULD NOT include more frames than fit in the MTU of the RTP transport protocol.
  • All frames in one packet MUST have the same length, clock rate and bit rate.
  • Frames MUST NOT be split between RTP packets.

The number of frames should suit the application. A telephony application, where delay matters, should use fewer frames per packet, while a delay-insensitive streaming or messaging application can use many.

The packet does not say how many frames it holds. A receiver counts the octets in the packet and divides by the expected octets per frame, which follows from the bit rate and therefore from the payload type.
sections.eli5: You can put several slices of sound in one parcel if they are all the same size, but you can never cut a slice in half. The receiver counts the parcel's weight to know how many slices are inside.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The document registers the media type audio/G7221. Its parameters are:

  • bitrate (required): the data rate of the stream, mandatory because the stream does not carry it. At the standard rates it MUST be 24000 or 32000 at 16 kHz, and 24000, 32000 or 48000 at 32 kHz.
  • rate (optional): the RTP timestamp clock rate, equal to the sampling rate. If missing, 16 kHz is assumed.
  • ptime and maxptime (optional): see RFC 4566; they SHOULD be multiples of 20 ms.

The type depends on RTP framing and is only defined for transfer via RTP.

In SDP, the media name in the m= line MUST be audio, the encoding name in a=rtpmap MUST be G7221, and rate goes in rtpmap as the clock rate. Only one bitrate SHALL be defined, using bitrate= in the a=fmtp line, for each payload type.

In the offer/answer model, the clock rate plus the bitrate define each payload type, and each configuration intended for use MUST be declared. RFC 3047 supports only 16 kHz, so a system that wants G.722.1 SHOULD offer a payload type with a clock rate of 16000 for backward interoperability.
sections.eli5: Before a call, each side writes a small note saying which sound format it will use and how fast. The note has to name exactly one speed for each label.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Packets in this format are subject to the security considerations of the RTP specification and any RTP profile in use. The main concerns are confidentiality, integrity and source authenticity. A suitable mechanism should provide confidentiality, integrity protection and at least source authentication.

No single mechanism is right for every case, since it depends on the application, transport and signaling. The RFC says SRTP is recommended if suitable, and that IPsec or TLS (for RTP over TCP) may also be used.

The payload format and its decoder show no significant non-uniformity in receiver-side computational complexity, so they are unlikely to enable denial of service through pathological data. The payload also contains no active content.
sections.eli5: Anyone could listen in or tamper with the parcels, so you need a lock and a signature. Which lock to use depends on how you are sending them.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 3047
sections.content:
This specification obsoletes RFC 3047. The main change is support for the superwideband (14 kHz) audio defined in annex C of the new revision of ITU-T G.722.1, which brings in the 32 kHz clock rate.

The text was also updated to follow the current rules for RFCs, and the media type registration now conforms to RFC 4288. Terminals SHOULD offer a media type at 16 kHz in order to interoperate with terminals that do not support the 32 kHz rate.
sections.eli5: This is the updated edition. It adds a higher-quality sound option while keeping the old option working.

data.title: Example offer
data.code:
m=audio 49000 RTP/AVP 121 122
a=rtpmap:121 G7221/16000
a=fmtp:121 bitrate=24000
a=rtpmap:122 G7221/32000
a=fmtp:122 bitrate=48000
